I am the project architect, and I want to tell you about the most expensive mistake I see on construction sites. It is not a design mistake. It is an old drawing. Somebody prints Revision B, pins it to the wall of the site office, and three weeks later the crew is still building from it, although Revision C changed the stair and a two-meter opening on the fourth floor. Nobody was careless. The new drawing simply never reached the person with the tape measure. So my rule is very simple. When a new revision arrives, the old drawings leave the site office the same day. And before any crew starts work, the foreman checks the revision letter in the title block. It takes thirty seconds.

On my second project as a site engineer, I was checking the drawings for a six-story office building, and I noticed something strange. The architectural plan showed a large opening in a wall on the ground floor, but on the structural drawings, the same wall was a load-bearing wall. My foreman wanted to start cutting on Monday. Instead, I flagged the discrepancy and sent an RFI to the structural engineer. He answered in two days. The architect had moved the opening in the last revision, and nobody had told the structure team. If we had cut that wall, we would have lost weeks, and maybe much more. Since then, I cross-reference every drawing before a crew touches anything.
